\chapter{Please}
\label{ch:hi-please}
\hlchaptermodality{8}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can say please in Hindi, both with \hi{कृपया} and with the polite verb ending everyday speech actually prefers.}

Say \hi{कृपया} with its vocalic \hi{ऋ}, unpack it as 'of your compassion', then switch to the everyday \hi{बैठिए}, 'please sit'.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[kṛpayā]{\hi{कृपया} (kṛpayā) — please (kindly)}

\label{lesson:HI-C08-kripaya}



\begin{quote}
Hindi's dictionary word for \textquotedblleft{}please\textquotedblright{} is really the word \textbf{compassion} in disguise — and it's more formal than you might expect.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know — The word}
\textbf{\hi{कृपया}} = \textbf{please}, literally \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{kindly / graciously}.\textquotedblright{} It's built on the Sanskrit noun \textbf{\hi{कृपा}} (\emph{kṛpā}), \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{grace, compassion, mercy}\textquotedblright{} — so asking with \emph{kṛpayā} means, at heart, \textquotedblleft{}of your compassion.\textquotedblright{}

That places Hindi in good company: \textbf{Arabic} asks \emph{min faḍlik} (\textquotedblleft{}from your \textbf{grace}\textquotedblright{}), and the Dravidian languages ask with \emph{daya} (\textquotedblleft{}\textbf{compassion}\textquotedblright{}). A whole swathe of Asia says \emph{please} by naming the kindness it hopes for — a different instinct from French's \textquotedblleft{}if it \textbf{pleases} you.\textquotedblright{}

The first letter hides a sound you met in the syllabary track: \textbf{\hi{कृ}} is \emph{ka} carrying the \textbf{vocalic r} (the \emph{\hi{ृ}} mark) — \emph{kṛ}, the same \emph{ṛ} vowel Sanskrit and the Dravidian scripts share.

\subsection*{You'll want to know — Be honest about how it's used}
Here's the catch a textbook often hides: \textbf{\hi{कृपया} is formal and bookish.} You'll see it on signs and hear it in announcements (\textquotedblleft{}\emph{kṛpayā} mind the gap\textquotedblright{}), but in everyday speech Hindi speakers rarely say it. Real politeness usually rides on \textbf{the verb} instead — the respectful request ending \textbf{‑\hi{इए} / ‑\hi{इएगा}} (\emph{-iye / -iyegā}): \emph{baiṭh\textbf{iye}} \textquotedblleft{}please sit,\textquotedblright{} \emph{sun\textbf{iye}} \textquotedblleft{}please listen.\textquotedblright{} And very often, people simply say the English word \textbf{\textquotedblleft{}please.\textquotedblright{}}

So learn \emph{kṛpayā} to \textbf{read} it and to be formally polite — but know that the living \textquotedblleft{}please\textquotedblright{} of Hindi is baked into the verb.

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}kṛpayā\textquotedblright{} — kṛ with the vocalic r, then -payā
  \item the root — \textquotedblleft{}kṛpā = compassion\textquotedblright{} $\to$ \textquotedblleft{}of your compassion\textquotedblright{}
  \item the everyday way — the verb ending: \textquotedblleft{}baiṭhiye\textquotedblright{} = \textquotedblleft{}please sit\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What is the formal Hindi word for please? (\textbf{\hi{कृपया}} \emph{kṛpayā}.) What does its root \emph{kṛpā} mean, and which other languages ask the same way? (\textbf{\textquotedblleft{}Grace / compassion\textquotedblright{}} — like Arabic \emph{min faḍlik} and Dravidian \emph{daya}.) Is \emph{kṛpayā} what people usually say out loud? (\textbf{No} — it's formal; everyday politeness rides on the verb ending \emph{-iye/-iyegā}, or people say English \textquotedblleft{}please.\textquotedblright{})
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[a]{\hi{अ} — one character, met inside words you already say}

\label{lesson:HI-S03-letter-a}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: \hi{न} — what does it do?

One character this time. Just one — and you have been saying it for pages without knowing which mark on the page it was.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script you'll notice: \hi{अ}}
\textbf{\hi{अ}} — \emph{a}.

It is an \textbf{independent vowel} — the shape the vowel \emph{a} takes when a word begins with it, rather than the sign it becomes inside a word.

What it is made of:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item a joined upper-and-lower left body
  \item a middle shoulder
  \item a right vertical stem
  \item the top shirorekhā
\end{itemize}

You already say these, and every one of them has \hi{अ} somewhere inside it:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{\hi{अलविदा}} — goodbye (alvidā — a final farewell, Persian/Arabic-derived)
\end{itemize}

\subsection*{Writing: \hi{अ}}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{1.} curve around the upper bowl, then continue down and around the lower bowl without lifting
  \item \textbf{2.} lift and sweep the middle shoulder right
  \item \textbf{3.} lift and draw the right stem top-to-bottom
  \item \textbf{4.} lift and draw the top shirorekhā left-to-right
\end{itemize}

\textbf{Pen lifts: 3.} The pen comes up 3 times and no more.

\begin{quote}
Verified modern printed teaching form; other Devanagari traditions split the body into more strokes.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
This is one attested teaching order and not a national standard — handwriting here is taught with school-to-school variation. Source: Saurmandal, ‘Devanagari \hi{अ} stroke order.svg’, frames 1–4, Wikimedia Commons, 5 August 2023.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Look:} at these words, and find \hi{अ} in the ones that have it
\end{itemize}

\begin{quote}
\hi{अलविदा}  ·  \hi{नमस्ते}
\end{quote}

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Trace it:} \hi{अ} three times, saying \emph{a} as you finish each one
  \item \emph{Look:} back at any page of this chapter and find \hi{अ} once more
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which character is this — \hi{अ}? What sound does it carry? (\emph{\textbf{a}}.) Name one word you already say that contains it.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[e]{\hi{◌े} — one character, met inside words you already say}

\label{lesson:HI-S112-vowel-sign-e}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: \hi{क} — what does it do?

One character this time. Just one — and you have been saying it for pages without knowing which mark on the page it was.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script you'll notice: \hi{◌े}}
\textbf{\hi{◌े}} — \emph{e}.

It is a \textbf{vowel sign}. It is not a letter and never stands alone: it attaches to a consonant and \textbf{replaces} the \emph{a} built into it with \emph{e}. Replaces, not adds — the \emph{a} is gone.

Where it sits: a stroke above the top bar.

Worked through: \textbf{\hi{म}} + \textbf{\hi{◌े}} = \textbf{\hi{मे}} — \emph{me}.

You already say these, and every one of them has \hi{◌े} somewhere inside it:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{\hi{नमस्ते}} \emph{namaste} — hello / goodbye (namaste — \textquotedblleft{}I bow to you\textquotedblright{})
  \item \textbf{\hi{शिरोरेखा}} \emph{shirorekhā} — the head-line that Devanagari letters hang from
  \item \textbf{\hi{मेरा}} \emph{merā} — my
  \item \textbf{\hi{मेरा} \hi{नाम}} \emph{merā nām} — assemble my name from known letters and show word spacing as two head-lines
\end{itemize}

\subsection*{Writing: \hi{◌े} — copy what you see}
Put your pen on \hi{◌े} and follow its line. Copy the shape you can see — slowly, and larger than it is printed.

\begin{quote}
This book does not yet tell you \textbf{where to start the character or which way to travel}. That is a real thing, taught with real variation from school to school, and it is not written down here until it can be written down with a source. Copying what is in front of you needs no such source, and it is how the shape gets into your hand in the meantime.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Look:} at these words, and find \hi{◌े} in the ones that have it
\end{itemize}

\begin{quote}
\hi{नमस्ते}  ·  \hi{शिरोरेखा}
\end{quote}

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Trace it:} \hi{◌े} three times, saying \emph{e} as you finish each one
  \item \emph{Look:} back at any page of this chapter and find \hi{◌े} once more
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which character is this — \hi{◌े}? What vowel does it put on the consonant it attaches to — and what does it take off? (\textbf{Puts \emph{e} on; takes the built-in \emph{a} off.}) Name one word you already say that contains it.
\end{tcolorbox}
